review:
The concepts behind this game are all great, you get to assemble a hangar full of war robots. You can customize your builds to fit your play style, select weapons from miniguns to rockets or energy weapons, be a sniper or chose to brawl it out with other players. This game copies and adds to ideas of another game that was very popular on mobile, War Robots (by the same company). 

Unfortunately, for some inexplicable reasons they decided to also copy many of the flaws of War Robots, and that's even before War Robots Frontiers managed to be released. As a result, I feel this was a good game that was killed even before it had a chance to take off. Here are the main problems with Frontiers:

1. Mobile revenue model (not yet in the game, but will come). Instead of paying once as it is with most PC games, this game will be "free" to play, meaning you'll have micro transactions. And with this company I can tell you right away the items you buy won't be cosmetic, it will be very egregious "pay for power" business model. 

2. Boggles my mind why they'd start this cycle of adding newer and more powerful content. They really had something great going with base builds and component customization. Each build had its own strength and weaknesses and almost all bots and weapons were viable to be used in combat. Now you know whatever is latest will be the most powerful so all your work in building and customizing your bot is out of the window. 
 
3. It was a mistake to add squad play so early, when the game has so few human players. The beginners will either experience tedious AI bot fights or matches where they are facing impossible odds against groups of experienced players. That's going to drive people away. The obvious solution is to make separate games for squads, but of course the devs will not consider it. 

4. Adding titans/alphas was a mistake too. Alpha is this super powerful version of your regular bot. And while this might sound good in principle, it completely messes up the balancing. Since you can wipe out many regular bots with your alpha, fielding and playing your alpha becomes the most important factor to winning the game. 

5. All current players need to be aware that their entire progress will be wiped out on release of this game. Many players, including myself, decided then to stay out for now. If this game is so equipment depended, why invest time to get something you'll lose?  

6. Paying to be essentially a tester. Not kidding. Eventually this game will be free, but for now while it's still in dev you have pay packages from 15$ all the way 99$. Now I don't mind supporting devs with few buck to support what might have been a great game, but 99$ for unfinished product in early access? Shows you the arrogance of this company.     

The result of the above problems is that this game that is supposed be multiplayer online shooter has currently 10-20 people playing, tops, across entire globe. Good luck finding a game with real human opponents. It's a great concept for a game but unfortunately was buried by all those monetization efforts.

It has potential. Robots movement and gunplay feels great. Gamepad and ultrawide screen support. Nice graphics.
Hope it won't become a shameless P2W without any balance. Hope Frontiers will shape to be a more premium game.

First, I've never played the original War Robots, so my experience is solely based on this game. 
I am enjoying it very much. The mechs are weighty and combat feels satisfying. The game is also running on Unreal Engine 5 so although the game already looks very good with very nice details on the mechs, weapons and environment it will look even better as the game gets closer to completion and engine's capabilities are fully realized. I see so much potential here for a highly competitive and approachable mech combat game. Only gripe is I wish movement speed, especially in the air was increased. If you jump and are in a combat area you'll be dead before you hit the ground, it's like your space jumping lol.

Currently there are about 10 robots to use parts from to make your own, and about 13 weapons to use. Weight capacity, speed, and energy (used to equip weapons/abilities) are determined by your choice of legs, and each chassis offers a unique ability (some even offering another weapon mount), while shoulders offer additional weapon mount locations. All parts have unique armor and health values. You can also unlock pilots by leveling that add some varying stats to your mech when equipped depending on your pilot choice.

You'll start the game with 3 armed robots and will have to play games to unlock additional parts. After a match you'll earn currency, about 900-1200 of it, or more if you earn MVP. New mech parts cost 2800 and new abilities (mods) cost 1700 so you can unlock a new part or ability every 2-3 games.

There is currently only one map, and although it is a good design, at only 13 hours in I'm already eager to play a new map. Matches are quick to find but are filled with bots if no players are found which personally I'm fine with rather than waiting and waiting for real people.

There is a rudimentary tutorial, which was fair enough to get an understanding of the game. There is no training/practice mode which i really hope they add sooner than later so we can tinker with various builds and have something to grind for that we know actually works. Nothing worse than spending your hard earned currency on a custom build that turns out isn't a very good combination.

The base concept of the game is cool - mix and match parts to make a custom robot with each part having different abilities and hardpoints. Each part in-game has its own armour, and once it depletes, getting hit in that part will do extra HP damage. I wish they would expand upon this mechanic a bit more, not like just attacking a part making it a weak point, but maybe something on top of that, like having your armour broken on your legs causing your robot to move slower.

Currently there are some obvious imbalances, for example the Scourges as light slot weapons are unmatched at CQC, even beating out Heavy weapons like Thunders. There's bullet travel in this game, however the high mobility of most bots coupled with a slow bullet velocity means that for most weapons you'll have to significantly lead your target even in close quarters.

Speaking of bot movement, I can't help but feel like the bots are too mobile with their animations, like they wobble around while dashing, becoming nearly horizontal with enough speed, it makes the bots feel weightless, which I don't think goes well with the whole idea of having massive mechs made of metal.

This all may sound negative, but these are the only things I have gripes with so far and I truly do think that this game can go somewhere.

There are some QOL additions that I'd like to have added, like showing the amount of currently alive players on each team similarly to mobile, as well as saving the order type for your inventory when you move off it.

As an old [i] War Robots [/i] mobile player and a recent re-visitor of the original game on PC, [i] War Robots: Frontiers [/i] is the game I hoped would some day be developed. With the core mechanics and style of [i] War Robots [/i] providing many hours of entertainment, I couldn't help but imagine what it would be like to transfer the foundation of [i] War Robots [/i] into a game with state of the art graphics, physics, and more importantly (to me at least), relatively high skill-cap gameplay.

So far, [i] War Robots: Frontiers [/i] has provided the characteristics mentioned above. Despite graphical improvements being listed as one of the areas of emphasis in the official EA [url=https://wrfrontiers.com/en/roadmap] development roadmap [/url], the game is already graphically detailed and appealing. While I will admit the physics are a bit janky in certain scenarios, moving around the map feels pretty good with fluid momentum and weightiness added to landings. 

Regarding skillful and rewarding gameplay, as it stands now (in the early stages of EA), [i] War Robots: Frontiers [/i] feels like a game that has potential. Whereas [i] War Robots [/i] has always operated with lock-on targeting, the targeting system in [i] War Robots: Frontiers [/i] removes the snap-on target lock and instead operates with free aim. This feature, in conjunction with realistic physics, shapes robot combat into a more dynamic and skill-based system. In addition to this, the capability to mix and match equal leveled weapons, robot parts, and abilities promotes creativity and a focus on improving individual skills.

Overall, as long as developers continue to interact with the community and implement positive additions to the game that don't lead it towards the current state of [i] War Robots [/i], I see [i] War Robots: Frontiers [/i] as a game with a lot of potential to become one of the best and most popular mech shooters.

So far, I really like this game! Not only does it look great, but the combat is buttery smooth. In the future, I would like to maybe throw out some ideas, although I'm aware that I'm nothing but one player out of many. (Mainly game modes). 

1. Battle against AI.
Adding a game mode that allows the play to fight only other AI would have a few benefits as of now. For a start, it would allow players to play rounds a lot quicker (As they would not be waiting for other players). Also, it would allow you to test your builds right when you make them, to truly get a feel for what game style works best for you. There are also some players that just might not want to be competitive, and would rather play a quick and calm match. In the future, you can allow every game mode to have an AI counterpart/option, instead of just the classic 6v6.

2. A no Titan game mode.
While I do enjoy using Titans, they can matches drag on. They seem nothing short of overpowered compared to your average robot, as just one Titan can easily kill multiple robots at once. I've been hearing a lot of people talking about how they strongly dislike Titans as a whole, and how they want Titans to be removed all together. However, I don't think this is the answer. Instead, you can add a game mode where Titans are disabled. This will please both sides of the argument, while allowing you to keep on making epic new Titans! As listed above, you can make an AI version of this game mode available.

3. A Boss fight of sorts.
In this game mode, you and a team of other players all come together to defeat a strong enemy, armed with many weapons and tricks. This could not only be a fun and alternate way to earn rewards, but this can also serve as way to find your build's weakness and strength. Also, I'm sure the bosses would look bad ass!

4. Battle among Titans.
The game mode is as the title says. You get to fight with your Titan, and your Titan only. I'll be honest, I'm not sure what advantages this will bring to your team, but it would be a cool way to test your titans. (This mode will work better once you start to make more Titans, at least I think).

5. FFA (Free For All).
A game mode where you are alone, fighting everyone else to live. This could be a great way to see how your robot can handle difficult places, like a 2v1. It would also add variety in general to the game.

That's all I have for now, thank you if you read this. I know that I'm not an expert or anything, I just thought this was worth sharing. But overall, great game so far!

So I was playing during the paid early access and enjoy a F2P game so let me break it down for you. 

Where is this game good: 
Movement and game play:
This is something they got right very early. Every robot gets a dash on shift and a jetpack jump that will be a determined by a few things but mostly based on the legs you are using. There are moments that can feel over the top in a way that's a little camp but in a good way. 

The bad: 
Time:
This F2P model wants you to put in 4-6 games everyday to get your tasks done. the weekly tasks are something along the lines of complete daily task X five times so get several games in 5 days a week. The currency's your given break down pretty poorly. You grind missions poorly for coins and you'll need several months of the grind to upgrade one robots parts.

Game modes:
If the daily tasks are something like capture a point but, there is no way to select a game mode that line up with your mission. In practice this leads to people just dropping games making a frustrating game you might need to play for progress. They have since added bots instead of punishing people for dropping games so it's not a guaranteed loss but bots are bad and band aid for a larger issue. Making you more Likely to have a bad game based on the f2p model. 

Value to dollar:
I think this is pretty poor on one side picking up the "premium time"  the difference is a little staggering somewhere in the 3.25 times faster progress on things like the parts you can make with a significant bump to the currency you earn by playing each game, xp leveling what parts you can build and doubling the number of daily challenges. One issue I have with it is the price to dollar for other stuff things such as robots and pilots are really missing the mark for me to be willing to put in money and I've spent on games like this.  

Customization:
The menus feel poorly optimized Eg. not being able to tab through your parts you need to go back a menu and then click back into them to open another menu to open an upgrade menu that I hope they work on at some point. A few issues here.
#1 The robots you build don't feel unique or fun to work on. There is little wiggle room from what they intend you to build and it makes for a pretty crap meta esp when you factor in cost to get the new over tuned guns before they nerf them down to a reasonable level the idea is nothing crazy but to make one gun two to three times the damage anything else can do to push people to get them feels bad. 
#2 All the mechs are on a similar frame Legs, torso, shoulder and guns with no spacers or parts to modify the silhouette which is weird because "War Robots" the phone game does this pretty well and can have a verity of things that are recognizable from a distance and adds a little something for you to be attached to weather its a look or specific game play thing they can do well. 
#3 The issue with camouflage being monetized. It's one thing to give a special skin for doing well in a season but that's not what this is things like basic colors and how decal are pushed (and applied) all being pushed for fomo. looking at games like Forza letting people spend time designing and layering decals and colors to good menu music and distribute those designs is something that's been proven to be enjoyed as a reason to spend more time in the game.  

Personal note: 
The developers have been around for a while. They know exactly what they're doing however you want to interpret that. The menus at the port / hanger / garage feel a little too much like a "World of" game for me and this game is lacking a unique feel to set it apart as it's own thing. As an early access supporter I wanted the game to do well but I will not encourage the people I games with to play this either with or without me. 

TLDR: 
Game play - Good
Monetization - Bad
Worth checking out - Yes 
Main game - No

Way too much power is given to camping, no skill, scaredy-cat hide behind a wall and lob rockets playstyles, that when people who know how to move and use tactics try to play there is not much you can do.

A game should always be balanced in such a way that if there is little risk, then you should get little reward.  That doesn't happen in this game.  Everyone uses the same weapons and torsos so that all they have to do is toss a rocket across the map revealing the location of the enemy team, and then cowardly and mindlessly lob rockets from behind a wall and do tons of damage.  The game is balanced so poorly its beyond comprehension. And every match goes like this and it just gets old.

- Graphics and sound are great
